Cevian Triangle

GeometryTrianglesConstructions
Game: Drag the point P or a corner of a triangle and watch a smaller triangle appear inside it.
How to play: Drag with a mouse or finger, or focus a dot and use the arrow keys. Press Show names to label the points and Check the theorem to test what you see.
Look for the math

Draw three lines through one point inside a triangle. They cut out a smaller triangle. Stretch the sides of both triangles and something surprising happens: three new meeting points fall on a single straight line.

One point, three lines

Start with triangle ABC and any point P. The line from A through P meets the opposite side BC at Pa; in the same way Pb lies on CA and Pc lies on AB. Lines like these are called cevians, and PaPbPc is the cevian triangle of P. Because each line A Pa, B Pb, C Pc passes through P, the two triangles are said to be perspective from a point. The logic test checks that all three feet really fall on their opposite sides, on hundreds of triangles with P inside and outside.

A straight line from two triangles

Now match the sides: let L = AB ∩ PaPb, M = BC ∩ PbPc and N = CA ∩ PcPa. Desargues' theorem says that two triangles perspective from a point are also perspective from a line: L, M and N are always collinear. That green line is the axis. The logic test compares all six intersections with a second transcription of the applet's own line-intersection method on hundreds of configurations, including P at a corner and P on a side. If two matching sides happen to be parallel, their meeting point runs off the picture (the old applet printed NaN); the axis is then the line through the other two points.

The orthic triangle

Put P at the orthocenter. The cevians become the altitudes, and the cevian triangle becomes the orthic triangle; its axis is called the orthic axis. The old page says the sides of ABC are external bisectors of the orthic triangle, and links Menelaus' theorem for the collinearity. Both are literally true for an acute triangle. In an obtuse triangle the same side line bisects the internal angle at two of the feet instead, so the page's wording is too narrow; the collinearity still holds. The logic test checks this on hundreds of acute and obtuse triangles.

Try dragging P close to a side, or make a long thin triangle: watch which of L, M and N shoots far away while the green line stays straight.
